Peter Payne
pee'ter pan
n. (Peter Payne, called Engliš, c. 1380–c. 1455, English Wycliffite who fled to Bohemia and became a Hussite spokesman at Basel)
Payne, English, from Old French paien, a countryman and so a heathen, a common surname; Engliš, the Czech by-name given him, the Englishman.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Peter Payne was an Oxford man and a convinced Wycliffite who, when the English authorities began to hunt Lollards in earnest, left the country about 1414 and went to Prague, where Wycliffe's books were honoured and his own were useful. He was admitted a master of the university, married, and lived the rest of his life as a Bohemian. He is the clearest personal link between the two movements: the Hussites had their Wycliffe from Oxford scholars and Czech students, and Payne was the Oxford scholar in the room. He argued the Hussite case in the disputations at Prague, served the movement as a diplomat on embassies to Poland and Lithuania, and in 1433 was one of the four Hussite spokesmen before the Council of Basel, where he was given the third of the Four Articles to defend—that the clergy should be stripped of worldly dominion and property. He inclined to the Taborite side, was imprisoned for a time by a Catholic lord and ransomed, and died in Bohemia about 1455. The dictionary enters him because the Reformation was never a national movement, whatever every nation has since claimed. A doctrine held in Oxford travelled in a student's satchel to Prague, and a hundred years later came back to England by way of Wittenberg.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an exile as one banished from his country; dominion as sovereign authority; and an advocate as one who pleads the cause of another.

expand to see more

EXILE, n. [L. exilium.] Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country by authority; the person banished.

DOMINION, n. [L. dominium.] Sovereign or supreme authority; the power of governing; territory under a government.

ADVOCATE, n. [L. advocatus.] One who pleads the cause of another in a court of judicature; one who defends or vindicates.

EMBASSY, n. The message or public function of an ambassador; the person or persons sent as ambassadors.

SCHOLAR, n. [L. scholaris.] One who learns of a teacher; a man of letters; one who has learning.

Key Scripture

Heb 11:13 — "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth."

1Pe 5:2 — "Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;"

Mat 5:10 — "Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."

Isa 8:20 — "To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them."

Modern Corruption

Oxford Wycliffite who became a Bohemian master and spoke for the Hussites at Basel on the stripping of the clergy of worldly dominion.

expand to see more

The corruption at issue in his article at Basel was clerical lordship: bishops holding counties, abbots holding armies, a priesthood that was also the greatest landowner in the kingdom. The Hussite complaint was not envy but order—that a man cannot feed a flock and farm a province, and that the wealth drew into the ministry exactly the men who should never be in it. “not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2) is the apostolic requirement, and a church whose preferments are worth fighting for in a royal court has made that requirement untestable.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that doctrine has no country. Modern writing on the Reformation is organised by nation, which is convenient and misleading. Payne's life shows the real shape of it: Oxford to Prague by way of a persecution, and Bohemian theology furnished with English books. The dictionary holds that the church is one across the nations and that the gospel is carried by refugees at least as often as by missions.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek parepidemos (G3927), a sojourner; Greek aischrokerdos (G146), from a love of base gain.

expand to see more

Greek xenos (G3581) — a stranger, a foreigner; “they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth”, Hebrews 11:13.

Greek peitho (G3982) — to persuade, to be persuaded; “and were persuaded of them”, Hebrews 11:13.

Greek aischrokerdos (G147) — for the sake of base gain; “not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind”, 1 Peter 5:2.

Greek dioko (G1377) — to pursue, to persecute; “persecuted for righteousness' sake”, Matthew 5:10.

Hebrew torah (H8451) — law, instruction; “To the law and to the testimony”, Isaiah 8:20.

Usage

"“they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb 11:13) — Oxford to Prague about 1414, and never home again."

"“not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2) — the third article defended at Basel in 1433."

"“Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake” (Mat 5:10) — the Lollard hunt that sent him abroad."
